historicalNarrative.text: Aušros Vartų parish and its church at 568-570 Broome Street emerged from Manhattan's Lithuanian immigrant community in the opening years of the twentieth century. The surviving record does not yield one uncontested founding date: contemporary and retrospective accounts variously point to a 1905 parish authorization or centennial, a December 1909 opening, and a 1910 building date. The public record therefore leaves the parish's founding year unresolved rather than choosing among them.

The yellow-brick Lombard-Gothic church was designed by Harry G. Wiseman and built with immigrant donations at a reported cost of $25,000. It became a Lithuanian Catholic anchor in lower Manhattan. Its later interior included stained-glass windows by Vytautas Kazimieras Jonynas, acquired in the 1980s from Brooklyn's closed Lithuanian Church of Our Lady Queen of Angels, so the building also carried sacred art rescued from an earlier lost parish.

The closing unfolded without a final liturgy. On January 19, 2007, Aušros Vartų was absent from the archdiocese's morning list of 21 parish closures, but a separate statement that evening said it would close anyway. On February 26, while pastor Eugene Sawicki was summoned to meet Cardinal Edward Egan, the locks were changed and a guard posted. Parishioners later entered the church on April 29 and found the interior stripped: the Jonynas windows were gone, the Marian icon had been removed, and a neighbor reported that pews had been trucked away before dawn.

The community answered the lockout with a sustained public campaign. Beginning March 4, 2007, parishioners gathered outside the locked church every Sunday for prayer, hymns, and what they called a virtual church; the gatherings continued for eight years. They delivered 396 signed petitions and more than 3,000 online statements, appealed to Lithuanian and American church leaders, and carried the case to President Valdas Adamkus, who raised it with Pope Benedict XVI on April 28, 2007. The pope told him he knew the case and would discuss it with the American bishops.

The fight proceeded on both canonical and civil tracks. Parishioners appealed to the Congregation for the Clergy on April 4, 2007 and later to the Apostolic Signatura; no published outcome of either canonical appeal has been found. A New York lawsuit stopped demolition in 2008, and an appellate stay preserved the building again in January 2009. In December 2011, however, the New York Court of Appeals entered the final civil ruling allowing the archdiocese to demolish it.

The Jonynas windows reached Marijampolė, Lithuania, on March 25, 2013, intended for a future church there. The Broome Street church itself was demolished in April 2015. At a farewell gathering on April 26, parishioners lit 105 candles for the building's 105 years; the following year Draugas confirmed that it had been completely razed that April. A condominium tower now occupies the site, but the former parish community continues to maintain its memorial record and support other endangered churches.

summary: Our Lady of Vilnius Church at 568-570 Broome Street was demolished in April 2015 — Draugas reported the demolition under way with a farewell gathering on April 26, 2015 (105 candles for the building's 105 years), and stated in 2016 that the building was 'galutinai nugriautas 2015 m. balandį' — four years after the NY Court of Appeals ruled for the archdiocese. Contemporary reports describe a 2013 sale to Extell and a 2014 resale for $18.4 million, but the printed buyer names and component prices are not fully consistent. A residential tower permit followed in August 2014. Today the site holds 570 Broome, a 25-story, 54-unit condominium designed by Tahir Demircioglu (Builtd) for Agime Group, completed in 2019; the building's marketing makes no mention of the church. The parish tabernacle went to the Church of the Blessed Kateri Tekakwitha and sacramental records to St. Anthony of Padua on Sullivan Street. The parishioner-run memorial blog remains active as of May 2026, now advocating for other endangered churches such as St. Mary's in Yonkers.

developments.headline: Church demolished — April 2015, resolved by the Draugas record
developments.detail: Draugas of April 30, 2015 (pp. 1, 4, Gitana Merkelienė, 'Griaunama Aušros Vartų bažnyčia') reported the demolition under way — crosses already gone from the towers, the building 'jau beveik sulygintas su žeme' — with a farewell gathering on April 26, 2015: 105 candles for the building's 105 years. A Draugas follow-up of August 25, 2016 (p. 5) states the building was 'galutinai nugriautas 2015 m. balandį.' A June 2020 Draugas item describing demolition 'in progress' is a recycled near-verbatim reprint of the April 2015 farewell report and is not evidence of a 2020 demolition. Tabernacle had gone to Blessed Kateri Tekakwitha church, records to St. Anthony of Padua.

developments.headline: The closure and the locking, from the scanned Draugas record
developments.detail: The scanned-era Draugas issues document the closure fight in real time. The first closure report ran September 28, 2006 (BNS): the archdiocese intended to close 'the last Lithuanian house of prayer in New York.' The announcement came in two stages on January 19, 2007 — the 10 a.m. realignment list of 21 closures did not include the parish; a 5 p.m. archdiocese statement said it would close anyway. On the morning of February 26, 2007, pastor Eugene Sawicki was summoned to meet Cardinal Egan; while he was away, the locks were changed and a guard posted. No closure date had been announced, and no final Mass was ever held. Parishioners held a candlelight vigil at the locked doors that evening, filed an appeal with the Congregation for the Clergy on April 4, 2007, and delivered 396 signed petitions plus over 3,000 online statements. On April 28, 2007 Benedict XVI told President Adamkus in a private audience that he would discuss the church with the US bishops. The Sunday gatherings at the locked doors became a weekly 'virtual church' that continued for eight years, until the demolition.
